items.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: I mean Charlie Parker was dead when he was 34, you know what I mean.

ctx.x: Yeah, his next gig. I like the way you said that, next gig. So like on the way we give respect and all of those kinds of things to the body on the way to the cemetery. We play dirges and quite naturally the family is sad, people who knew this person is sad, and when we get to the cemetery, we play a nice slow hymn, some kind of hymn, “What a Friend We Have in Jesus,” or “Goodbye Charlie” or whatever it’s going to be. And then we immediately turn around and start the celebration. Because this guy has gone on…
And the music is a large part of that. It helps them do that.

items.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 16, 2000 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Charlie Parker was in the band [Jay McShann band]... And it’s just kind of like prelude to Bebop. I mean it’s just like, and in some ways the introduction was more complex than the tune itself. You know? Like some of those, like on “Salt Peanuts,” [scats] man that’s some bad stuff man.

ctx.x: Who has the Olympia Brass Band. That was my dad’s first cousin. And he went up there and he auditioned for Juilliard and he won a scholarship to Juilliard. So when he was 16 he was at Juilliard. And by the time he was 19, I don’t know if he had graduated or if he had left, I don’t know what the thing was, but my mom’s mother had died so he came back to New Orleans, they got married, and he started touring with, I think it was the Jay McShann band at first. And he wrote some arrangements, Charlie Parker was in the…
Oh gee, I didn’t know that.
